Chief Executive’s Monthly Management Report – 30th April 2026
 
 
A Chara,  
 
I enclose the above report for your statutory consideration, this report has also been prepared under Section 136 & 
138 of the Local Government Act, 2001. The attached report is the Chief Executive’s Monthly Management Report for 
April 2026, detailing activities, updates, and progress across various departments of Louth County Council. Below is 
a summary of key achievements and actions under various directorates from the Chief Executive Report for April 
2026: 
 
1. Financial Management and System Support 
• 
Financial position to 30th April 2026: total expenditure €57.6m against budget €203.7m (28%). Income €75.6m 
invoiced/received against budget €203.7m (37%). 
• 
772 ICT support calls logged during April; 90% completed.  Security and application software were the highest 
request categories. 
• 
GIS public service: Dowdallshill Graveyard Map Viewer recorded 2,211 views (average 76/day) and was 
updated to include burial information from 2020. 
• 
Cyber security training: staff guidance emphasised verifying urgent/unexpected requests via trusted channels 
and avoiding link-clicking/credential sharing. 
 
2. Economic Delivery 
• 
Key updates include new chair appointment to the Louth Economic Forum; SPC progress with the Tourism 
Strategy moving toward Council approval;  
• 
Shopfront Improvement Grant Scheme updated rules and open for 2026;  
• 
Tourism and business events supported (e.g. cross-border tourism conference, town leadership summit); and 
ongoing enterprise supports (mentoring, clinics, training, and grant approvals). 
• 
Age Friendly Business, plus events that promote place-based economic activity. 
• 
For the month of March 2026, 81 planning applications received during the month of which 74 were valid.  In 
addition, there were 20 responses received during the month to requests for further information and 23 Pre-
Planning Requests received. 
 
3. Operations and Environmental Delivery 
• 
The report Includes extensive operational updates by municipal area (Dundalk/North Louth, Mid Louth/Ardee, 
Drogheda/South Louth) covering roadworks, drainage, sweeping, footpaths, signage, traffic lights, and 
responses to illegal dumping.  
• 
Environmental enforcement and regulation reporting includes litter/waste investigations and notices, pollution 
complaints (water/air/noise), landfill monitoring, septic tank queries, and related inspections. 
• 
Successful award of €20,000 Heritage Council funding for the development and delivery of a Local Biodiversity 
Action Plan. 
• 
In 2025, the Council reduced CO₂ emissions by 431 tonnes. A further reduction is targeted of 1,682 tonnes to 
meet the 2030 target. 
• 
17 of 21 total sites on the project to increase Solar PV to its buildings, this gives 515 kilowatts of renewably 
generated PV panels and battery storage equipment, has been added to Council building stock. 
• 
Great progress on the Dundalk’s new Athletics Track at Muirhevnamór Sports Centre substantial completion 
of the works is anticipated in June. 
 
4. HR, Corporate & Community Delivery  
• 
In April 2026 Customer Services dealt with 13,432 queries inclusive of 6,669 calls and 6,763 counter queries. 
9,406 (70%) of queries received were dealt with at first point of contact. 
• 
April 30th was National Voter Registration Day, which was a nationwide initiative promoting active citizenship 
by encouraging everyone to ensure they are registered to vote. 
• 
Continued support for community activities, older people council, Age Friendly, Cooley Farming Community 
club, traveller development, LCDC and Comhairle na nÓg 
• 
LCDC, approved capital funding of €239,207.33 to 82 local community & voluntary groups in Louth, through 
the Local Enhancement Programme 2026. The LAG, approved funding support, of €103,462.98 for 2 LEADER 
projects.  To date, total funding allocated is €1,366,170.99, which is 37% of the total programme budget.

•

• 
Longwalk Urban Framework Plan: nearing completion 
• 
New Compulsory Purchase Orders (CPOs) are being initiated, acknowledged as lengthy but preparatory work 
is progressing. 
•

o

o

o

•

I would like to conclude by expressing my sincere appreciation for the exceptional commitment, resilience, and 
professionalism demonstrated by the entire Louth County Council team. Across all directorates, staff continued to 
deliver high-quality public services, maintain critical operations, and support our communities with dedication and 
pride. I encourage all members to read the report in full, which reflects the breadth, depth and impact of the remarkable 
work carried out across the organisation.

Cyber Security Training  
The April cyber security training highlighted the increasing sophistication of cyber threats, which often combine 
emails, phone calls and text messages to appear legitimate and bypass controls such as multi-factor 
authentication. Staff were reminded to treat urgent or unexpected requests with caution, even where messages 
appear convincing or reference personal or organisational details. The key message was clear: do not click links 
or share credentials in response to unsolicited communications, and always verify requests via a trusted, 
independent channel. Ongoing staff awareness and prompt reporting remain critical defences against cyber 
incidents.

night-time economy.  The training supports

businesses and organisations build public trust — 
which is essential for a strong and sustainable 
night-time economy and good for business.  The 
resource is easy to access, and participants receive 
a certificate upon completion.  The initiative’s 
progress is also easy to monitor and track. 
 
Due to the importance of the topic, the programme 
is being made available county-wide to ensure 
consistent standards, whilst developing Drogheda in 
the longer term as a regional centre of excellence.

Phase 2 – Built-up and Urban Areas (Key 
Points) 
• 
Phase 2 of the Irish National Speed Limit 
Review proposes introducing a default 
30km/h speed limit in built-up and urban 
areas, 
particularly 
in 
town 
centres, 
residential roads, areas with high numbers 
of vulnerable road users, and roads near 
schools (Urban School Zones), with limited 
exceptions. 
 
• 
However, implementation challenges were 
identified. There is no legislative definition 
of an “urban area” for speed-limit purposes, 
meaning new legislation would be required, 
delaying nationwide rollout. Existing legal 
definitions under the Local Government Act 
2001 identify only 85 built-up areas 
nationally, just three in County Louth 
(Dundalk, Drogheda and Ardee). These 
boundaries are outdated and no longer 
reflect current urban expansion. 
 
• 
In contrast, the CSO identifies 867 urban 
areas nationally, so changing the default 
built-up speed limit would only affect a 
small number of locations. The remaining 
areas would still require Special Speed 
Limit Bye-Laws.

Age Friendly Louth are collaborating with the HSE &

strong social aspect to it with elements of health and 
wellbeing, farming information, community information

supported by Age Friendly Louth & Louth Sports
